mechanism: Additive negative chronotropy, dromotropy and inotropy: non-dihydropyridine calcium-channel blockers (verapamil, diltiazem) plus beta-blockers can cause severe bradycardia, AV block or worsening heart failure; risk is highest with IV administration or pre-existing conduction disease/LV dysfunction.

management.prescriber_action: Verify the combination is intended and specialist-directed; assess heart rate, blood pressure, PR interval/conduction and LV function before continuing.
management.monitoring: Heart rate, blood pressure, ECG (PR interval) and signs of heart failure; more intensive for a new combination or dose increase.
management.patient_counselling: Report dizziness, fainting, very slow pulse, breathlessness or ankle swelling.
management.exceptions: Do not independently stop an established specialist-directed regimen; escalate any new, unexplained or symptomatic pairing. IV co-administration carries the highest risk of asystole.

evidence.excerpt: <verify — concomitant beta-blockers and verapamil have additive effects on heart rate, AV conduction and cardiac contractility>
evidence.normalized_proposition: Verapamil (a non-dihydropyridine CCB) plus a beta-blocker causes additive bradycardia, AV block and negative inotropy.

management_override.monitoring: Hepatic impairment raises verapamil/diltiazem levels; monitor heart rate and conduction more closely.
Renally cleared beta-blockers (e.g. atenolol, sotalol, nadolol) accumulate; monitor heart rate more closely.

mechanism: Two concerns: (1) additive bradycardia/AV-nodal slowing and hypotension during concurrent use; (2) on clonidine withdrawal, unopposed alpha-adrenergic activity causes rebound hypertension, which a concurrent (especially non-selective) beta-blocker can worsen.

management.prescriber_action: During coadministration monitor for bradycardia/hypotension. If therapy is being stopped, do NOT stop clonidine abruptly; withdraw the beta-blocker several days before tapering clonidine (prescriber-directed sequence).
management.monitoring: Heart rate and blood pressure; during any planned discontinuation monitor blood pressure closely for rebound hypertension.
management.patient_counselling: Do not stop clonidine suddenly; report very slow pulse, dizziness, or a severe/rapid rise in blood pressure (headache, palpitations).
management.exceptions: Combination may be intentional; do not unilaterally stop either drug — clarify the intended discontinuation sequence with the prescriber.

evidence.excerpt: <verify — beta-blockers may exacerbate rebound hypertension after clonidine withdrawal; discontinue the beta-blocker several days before withdrawing clonidine>
evidence.normalized_proposition: Beta-blocker plus clonidine adds bradycardia risk and, on clonidine withdrawal, can worsen rebound hypertension; the beta-blocker should be stopped first.

management_override.monitoring: Clonidine and renally cleared beta-blockers accumulate in renal impairment; monitor heart rate and blood pressure more closely.

mechanism: Verapamil inhibits P-glycoprotein, reducing digoxin clearance and raising serum digoxin (commonly by 50-75%) with risk of digoxin toxicity; additive AV-nodal slowing/bradycardia compounds the hazard.

management.prescriber_action: Obtain a baseline digoxin level; prescriber reduces the digoxin dose (commonly by ~50%) when starting verapamil and rechecks the level.
management.monitoring: Serum digoxin level, heart rate, renal function and electrolytes; watch for toxicity (nausea, visual disturbance, arrhythmia).
management.patient_counselling: Report nausea, vomiting, visual disturbance (yellow/green halos), confusion or palpitations.
management.exceptions: Digoxin is often established therapy — do not stop it unilaterally; flag for prescriber dose review and level check.

evidence.excerpt: <verify — verapamil increases serum digoxin concentrations; reduce digoxin dose and monitor>
evidence.normalized_proposition: Verapamil raises serum digoxin via P-glycoprotein inhibition, risking toxicity.

management_override.prescriber_action: Reduced renal function markedly raises digoxin toxicity risk; withhold and confirm the digoxin dose/level plan before supply.

mechanism: Amiodarone inhibits P-glycoprotein and reduces digoxin renal/biliary clearance, roughly doubling serum digoxin, with additive bradycardia/AV block; onset is delayed and the effect prolonged owing to amiodarone's long half-life.

management.prescriber_action: Obtain a baseline digoxin level; prescriber reduces the digoxin dose (commonly by ~50%) and rechecks the level; the interaction persists for weeks after amiodarone is changed.
management.monitoring: Serum digoxin level, heart rate, renal function and electrolytes; watch for toxicity (nausea, visual disturbance, arrhythmia).
management.patient_counselling: Report nausea, vomiting, visual disturbance (yellow/green halos), confusion or palpitations.
management.exceptions: Digoxin is often established therapy — do not stop it unilaterally; flag for prescriber dose review and level check.

evidence.excerpt: <verify — amiodarone increases serum digoxin concentrations; reduce digoxin dose by about half and monitor>
evidence.normalized_proposition: Amiodarone raises serum digoxin via P-glycoprotein inhibition (delayed, prolonged), risking toxicity.

management_override.prescriber_action: Reduced renal function markedly raises digoxin toxicity risk; withhold and confirm the digoxin dose/level plan before supply.

mechanism: Dronedarone inhibits P-glycoprotein, increasing serum digoxin, with additive AV-nodal slowing; the dronedarone label advises halving or discontinuing digoxin.

management.prescriber_action: Obtain a baseline digoxin level; prescriber halves or discontinues digoxin per the dronedarone label and rechecks the level.
management.monitoring: Serum digoxin level, heart rate, renal function and electrolytes; watch for toxicity (nausea, visual disturbance, arrhythmia).
management.patient_counselling: Report nausea, vomiting, visual disturbance (yellow/green halos), confusion or palpitations.
management.exceptions: Digoxin is often established therapy — do not stop it unilaterally; flag for prescriber dose review and level check.

evidence.excerpt: <verify — dronedarone increases digoxin exposure; halve or discontinue digoxin and monitor>
evidence.normalized_proposition: Dronedarone raises serum digoxin via P-glycoprotein inhibition, risking toxicity.

management_override.prescriber_action: Reduced renal function markedly raises digoxin toxicity risk; withhold and confirm the digoxin dose/level plan before supply.

mechanism: Clarithromycin inhibits P-glycoprotein and suppresses gut flora (Eggerthella lenta) that inactivate digoxin, raising serum digoxin; serious/fatal toxicity has been reported, especially in the elderly and in renal impairment.

management.prescriber_action: Consider an antibiotic without this interaction where clinically appropriate; if clarithromycin is used, monitor the digoxin level and consider a temporary dose reduction.
management.monitoring: Serum digoxin level, renal function and heart rate; watch for toxicity during the course and for a few days after.
management.patient_counselling: Report nausea, vomiting, visual disturbance, confusion or palpitations.
management.exceptions: Short antibiotic course — do not stop established digoxin; manage via antibiotic choice, level check and dose adjustment.

evidence.excerpt: <verify — clarithromycin increases serum digoxin concentrations; monitor for digoxin toxicity>
evidence.normalized_proposition: Clarithromycin raises serum digoxin via P-glycoprotein inhibition and gut-flora suppression, risking toxicity.

management_override.prescriber_action: Reduced renal function markedly raises digoxin toxicity risk; withhold and confirm the digoxin dose/level plan or an alternative antibiotic before supply.

mechanism: Loop and thiazide diuretics can cause hypokalaemia and hypomagnesaemia, which potentiate digoxin binding at the Na/K-ATPase and precipitate toxicity even at therapeutic serum digoxin levels; diuretic-induced volume/renal changes can also raise digoxin levels.

management.prescriber_action: Use recent/actual serum potassium and magnesium to gauge risk; correct and maintain K+ and Mg2+; consider potassium-sparing strategy or supplementation as clinically appropriate.
management.monitoring: Serum potassium, magnesium, renal function and digoxin level; heart rate/rhythm.
management.patient_counselling: Report palpitations, nausea, visual disturbance, weakness or confusion.
management.exceptions: Documented recent normal potassium and magnesium lowers the concern; this is not automatically high-severity for every digoxin+diuretic pair.

evidence.excerpt: <verify — hypokalaemia and hypomagnesaemia predispose to digoxin toxicity; monitor and correct electrolytes>

management_override.prescriber_action: Renal impairment worsens both digoxin accumulation and electrolyte derangement; withhold and confirm recent electrolytes and digoxin level/dose plan before supply.

mechanism: Strong CYP3A4 inhibitors markedly increase ivabradine exposure, exaggerating bradycardia and the risk of conduction disturbance/serious arrhythmia; co-administration with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors is a labelled contraindication.

management.prescriber_action: Do not co-supply; select a non-interacting alternative for either drug, or defer ivabradine until the strong inhibitor course is complete.
management.monitoring: If exposure has already occurred, monitor heart rate/ECG for bradycardia.
management.patient_counselling: Report very slow pulse, dizziness, fainting or transient visual brightness (phosphenes).
management.exceptions: Applies to strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (e.g. ketoconazole/itraconazole, clarithromycin, ritonavir/cobicistat, nefazodone). Most moderate CYP3A4 inhibitors are a separate dose-limited caution; however verapamil and diltiazem (heart-rate-lowering moderate inhibitors) are contraindicated with ivabradine under EMA/UK labelling and to be avoided under US labelling — they are NOT merely an additive-risk pairing.

evidence.excerpt: <verify — concomitant use with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors is contraindicated>
evidence.normalized_proposition: Ivabradine is contraindicated with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors owing to increased exposure and bradycardia risk.

management_override.prescriber_action: Ivabradine is independently contraindicated in severe hepatic impairment; do not supply.

mechanism: Ivabradine lowers heart rate, and bradycardia is itself a risk factor for torsades de pointes; combined with QT-prolonging or other heart-rate-lowering agents the bradycardia/arrhythmia risk is additive and should be weighed on patient risk (baseline QTc, electrolytes, bradycardia, structural heart disease).

management.prescriber_action: Assess baseline heart rate, QTc, electrolytes and the specific TdP risk of the co-prescribed agent; avoid stacking where the added agent is a known torsades risk.
management.monitoring: Heart rate, ECG/QTc and electrolytes as clinically indicated.
management.patient_counselling: Report palpitations, fainting, dizziness or very slow pulse.
management.exceptions: Distinct from the strong-CYP3A4-inhibitor contraindication rule; here the concern is additive bradycardia/QT, weighed on patient risk factors. NOTE: verapamil and diltiazem must NOT be down-tiered into this additive class — they are contraindicated with ivabradine under EMA/UK labelling (avoid under US labelling) and require handling as a contraindication.

evidence.excerpt: <verify — ivabradine causes bradycardia; use caution with other heart-rate-lowering drugs>
evidence.normalized_proposition: Ivabradine adds bradycardia/QT risk when combined with other QT-prolonging or heart-rate-lowering drugs.

management_override.prescriber_action: Ivabradine is independently contraindicated in severe hepatic impairment; do not supply.

mechanism: Dipyridamole blocks cellular reuptake/deamination of adenosine, potentiating and prolonging its effects (profound bradycardia, AV block, hypotension). This is a procedural/administration interaction — adenosine is given IV during a procedure — not an outpatient co-dispensing hazard.

management.prescriber_action: Notify the team administering adenosine that the patient is on dipyridamole; a substantially lower adenosine dose is used (dipyridamole potentiates the effect). For dipyridamole/adenosine-based pharmacologic stress testing, withhold dipyridamole beforehand per local protocol.
management.monitoring: Continuous ECG, heart rate and blood pressure during and after adenosine administration.
management.patient_counselling: Tell the procedural team about all current medicines, including dipyridamole or aspirin-dipyridamole combinations.
management.exceptions: Not an outpatient dispense-time block; the pharmacist action is to communicate the interaction to the administering/procedural team.

evidence.excerpt: <verify — dipyridamole potentiates the effect of adenosine; a lower adenosine dose may be required>
evidence.normalized_proposition: Dipyridamole potentiates and prolongs adenosine's effects, requiring adenosine dose reduction during administration.
